newsitem.title: USA: More Sherritt executives face U.S. travel ban.
newsitem.headline: More Sherritt executives face U.S. travel ban.

text.p: Four more executives of Canadian mining concern Sherritt International Corp. are to be banned from entering the United States because of company operations in Cuba, the State Department said on Friday.

Spokesman Nicholas Burns said the department was writing the executives on Friday informing them "that they will no longer 45 days after the receipt of the letters be welcome in the United States." He said a total of 11 Sherritt executives had now been barred.
The move stems from the U.S. Helms-Burton law providing for sanctions against foreign companies that utilize assets seized from U.S. citizens by Cuba's communist government.

Sherritt owns 50 percent of a nickel-cobalt mine in Moa Bay in eastern Cuba in a joint venture with the Havana government. The U.S. government says the mine, which was nationalized after the 1959 Cuban revolution, was "stolen" from the U.S. Moa Bay Mining Corp., now known as Freeport-McMoRan Inc., based in New Orleans.

"Sherritt now makes money off an American investment that was stolen by the Cuban government," Burns told a news briefing. "The Cuban government never compensated the Moa Bay Corporation or its successor."
Deploring the U.S. action, Canadian International Trade Minister Art Eggleton said in Ottawa: "I think it's a sorry situation, and I think it continues to be a violation of trade rules."
Eggleton said the United States was reaching a "new low" by "getting down to the employee level" at Sherritt.

Other board members of Toronto-based Sherritt were barred from the United States last July. Burns said the latest four, whom he declined to name, were not previously known to have been on the board and might be new members.
Helms-Burton was passed last year after Cuban fighters shot down two light aircraft flown by Cuban-Americans off the coast of Cuba, killing four people.

The only other company which has had executives banned from the United States under the law is the Mexican telecommunications firm Grupo Domos, although about a dozen firms have been warned they could face action.

President Bill Clinton has twice suspended a section of the act that allows U.S. citizens to sue foreign companies that utilize their former property in Cuba. Nevertheless the law has been fiercely criticized by Canada, Mexico and the European Union, which has threatened to take Washington to the World Trade Organization over it.
Eggleton said Canada would pursue joining the EU in its WTO challenge, suggesting the EU had gained nothing in its private discussions with Washington on the issue.
Burns on Friday defended the act as aimed against "companies that waltz in and take over stolen goods."

In a related dispute, lawyers for U.S. retailing giant Wal-Mart Stores Inc. were talking to the Treasury Department about whether Wal-Mart may sell Cuban-made pajamas in Canada, a Treasury official said on Friday.

The Canadian government has pressured Wal-Mart Canada into putting the cotton pajamas back on store shelves, putting the retailer in breach of U.S. laws aimed at bringing economic pressure against President Fidel Castro's government.
But Treasury, which is in charge of enforcing an embargo against any U.S.-owned company's trade with Cuba, appeared determined to ensure that American law was obeyed.
"Our interest is in enforcing the embargo," said Howard Schloss, Treasury's assistant secretary for public affairs.
